cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Memory – the mental power to store and recall past experiences.

p.em: Example: A good memory is essential for learning new vocabulary.

cosy-blockquote.p: Concrete – existing in a material or physical form; real and solid.

p.em: Example: 'Apple' is a concrete noun, while 'love' is abstract.

cosy-blockquote.p: Abstract – existing as an idea or quality, not a physical object.

p.em: Example: 'Freedom' is an abstract concept that is hard to visualize.

cosy-blockquote.p: Recall – to bring a fact or memory back into one's mind.

p.em: Example: I struggled to recall his phone number in the emergency.

cosy-blockquote.p: Visual – relating to seeing or sight.

p.em: Example: Creating a visual image of a word helps you remember it.

cosy-blockquote.p: Association – a mental connection between ideas, words, or things.

p.em: Example: We have a strong association between red and danger.

cosy-blockquote.p: Noun – a word used to identify any of a class of people, places, or things.

p.em: Example: Concrete nouns are much easier for language learners.

cosy-blockquote.p: Familiar – well known from long or close association.

p.em: Example: He felt comfortable because the settings were familiar.

cosy-blockquote.p: Experiment – a scientific procedure undertaken to make a discovery.

p.em: Example: The university conducted an experiment on word memory.

cosy-blockquote.p: Result – a consequence or outcome of an action or process.

p.em: Example: The experiment's result proved that concrete words are memorable.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
According to the article, how does the brain's memory system separate real compound words from fake ones like 'shamrock'?
★ What is your favorite word game or puzzle to play?

What evidence presented in the study makes it clear that a concrete word is processed faster than a pseudo-compound?
★ Do you find compound words easy to learn in a foreign language?

According to the study, what neural pathways are used when processing an abstract word instead of a physical object?
★ Have you ever had to decipher a very long, complex word in another language?

Based on the research findings, why is the brain able to recall 'football' faster than single or pseudo-compound terms?
★ Do you consider yourself a fast reader, or do you prefer to take your time?

According to the researchers, how does a visual mask help us measure subconscious word recognition in milliseconds?
★ What language structures do you find most beautiful or logical?

What kind of neurological association does the brain make when it breaks down a compound word?
★ Have you ever noticed yourself making subconscious links between unrelated words?

How does the study compare the cognitive workload of processing a compound noun versus a single noun?
★ How do you usually remember new vocabulary: by writing it down, or saying it?

What makes a familiar word structure significantly easier for our neural pathways to dismantle subconsciously?
★ Do you prefer reading physical books or reading on digital screens?

What specific scientific controls were put in place during the experiment to isolate word recognition speeds?
★ Have you ever noticed typos or misspelled words in books or articles immediately?

What main result from the study shows that we process language components subconsciously in milliseconds?
★ How do you personally break down a long sentence to understand its meaning?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
If future research confirms that the subconscious mind stores every word in a unified memory, we will use neural interfaces to read and understand books instantly.
★ Would you wear a neural device if it doubled your reading speed instantly?

As our understanding of brain processing develops, we will use cognitive chips to double our speed of processing a concrete word.
★ Do you think written language will eventually abandon complex grammar in favor of speed?

Imagine future research proves that speed-reading modifies our neural pathways; written language will eventually abandon an abstract vocabulary in favor of visual symbols.
★ Can artificial intelligence ever understand the emotional weight behind human word choices?

If researchers can fully map how we recall compound words, artificial intelligence will predict the subconscious links we make between words.
★ Would you like to be able to study a language by transferring vocabulary to your brain while sleeping?

As neural tracking technologies continue to advance, we will utilize a visual calibration system to cure dyslexia and other reading difficulties permanently.
★ Do you think real-time translators will eventually make learning foreign languages obsolete?

Imagine future research shows that a symbolic association is processed twice as fast as letters; future humans will communicate using visual symbols instead of letters.
★ Should future education focus more on speed-reading or deep, slow reading comprehension?

If future scientists discover how to inject a compound noun directly into brain pathways, we will be able to transfer vocabulary directly during sleep.
★ If human language evolved to be purely visual (like emojis), would we lose our intellectual depth?

As real-time audio translation chips are integrated into the auditory cortex, our familiar tongues will become obsolete.
★ Would you trust an AI to customize articles specifically to fit your reading speed?

If we can monitor cognitive latency in real time using a standard experiment, computers will write articles customized for our unique cognitive speed.
★ Do you think technology has shortened our attention spans for reading long texts?

As cognitive training models are validated by neuroimaging, a brain-boosting result will be standard in future education systems to optimize recognition.
★ What is the most difficult book you have ever read, and what made it so challenging?
